This development computes their degrees and prime-splitting behavior, then uses them to study genus theory of quadratic fields. The genus field describes the elementary two-part of the class group. These explicit constructions provide a calculable entry point into the relationship between class groups and unramified extensions.
tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/OneParameterSemig: One-parameter semigroups describe continuous evolution generated by possibly unbounded operators. This development studies generators, resolvents, the Hille–Yosida and Lumer–Phillips theorems, and abstract Cauchy problems. Parallel branches investigate completely monotone and positive-definite functions through Bernstein and Bochner representation theorems. Together these tools connect functional analysis with evolution equations, harmonic analysis and the operators arising in probability.
tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/OptimalTransport: Optimal transport asks how to move one probability distribution to another at minimum cost. This development builds transport plans, existence and Kantorovich duality, then studies Wasserstein geometry, optimal maps and Monge–Ampère equations. Dynamic formulations and metric gradient flows connect transport to evolution equations. Barycenters, entropic transport, Schrödinger bridges and synthetic curvature extend the theory to further geometric and probabilistic settings.
tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/PDE: Partial differential equations connect differential operators to boundary conditions, geometry and time evolution. This development builds domain Sobolev spaces, traces and compactness, alongside harmonic-analysis estimates and maximum principles. Energy methods give elliptic existence, followed by weak and classical regularity theories. Parabolic equations, semigroups and evolution methods extend the framework to dynamics and provide analytic foundations for other geometric and probabilistic developments.
tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/ReductiveGroups: Reductive algebraic groups provide the symmetry groups underlying much of representation theory and the Langlands program. This development connects group schemes, coordinate Hopf algebras and representations, then studies tori, unipotent groups, radicals and reductivity. Roots, parabolic subgroups and structure theory lead toward classification. Integral root data and pinned Chevalley–Demazure groups extend the picture from fields to group schemes over the integers.
tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/RepresentationThe: Representation theory studies algebraic and topological symmetry through linear actions. This collection links semisimple algebras and finite-group characters with induction, symmetric groups, quivers and highest-weight theory. Root systems and Lie groups provide the structural framework, while compact groups, classical groups and spin representations add analytic and geometric forms of the theory. The connections show how shared algebraic ideas support many distinct classification problems.

Characters compress finite-group representations into class functions while retaining their decomposition into irreducibles. This development constructs character tables, orthogonality relations, central idempotents and the arithmetic of character values. The class algebra supports a certified Burnside–Dixon–Schneider algorithm with exact cyclotomic output. Frobenius–Schur indicators, Frobenius groups and representations of GL₂ over finite fields supply structural results and worked families.

Representations of classical groups can be built concretely from tensor powers of their standard representations. This development uses Young symmetrizers and highest weights to study the general linear, special linear, orthogonal and symplectic groups. Schur polynomials and Weyl's dimension formula describe characters and dimensions. Branching rules and Gelfand–Tsetlin bases explain how representations decompose when restricted to smaller groups.

Compactness makes averaging available and gives continuous representations a rich orthogonal structure. This development uses normalized Haar measure to construct invariant inner products, complete reducibility and matrix coefficients. Schur orthogonality leads to the Peter–Weyl theorem, describing square-integrable functions on a compact group in terms of irreducible representations. Characters and the example of SU₂ connect the analysis to concrete Lie theory.

Induction and restriction relate the representations of a group to those of its subgroups. This development constructs their compatibility laws and induced characters, then develops Frobenius reciprocity, Mackey decomposition and irreducibility criteria. Clifford theory treats normal subgroups, while Artin and Brauer induction organize virtual characters. Projective representations and the Schur multiplier extend the framework to actions defined up to scalar.

Lie groups connect smooth geometry with algebra through their tangent Lie algebras. This development constructs exponential maps, one-parameter subgroups and the adjoint action, then proves the closed-subgroup theorem and integrates Lie algebras to groups. Maximal tori, Weyl groups and integration formulas describe compact structure. Complexification, flag manifolds and Cartan and Iwasawa decompositions connect the theory to representation theory and symmetric spaces.

Highest weights classify the finite-dimensional irreducible representations of semisimple Lie algebras. This development starts with sl₂, roots and weight spaces, then constructs enveloping algebras, Verma modules and irreducible highest-weight modules. Complete reducibility and the Weyl character and dimension formulas make the classification effective. Central characters, Kostant's formulas, exceptional examples and reductive extensions deepen the structure and its computational consequences.

A quiver representation assigns vector spaces to vertices and linear maps to arrows, turning a diagram into an algebraic object. This development relates those representations to modules over path algebras and establishes decomposition theory. Dimension vectors, Euler forms and reflection functors lead to Gabriel's classification of finite representation type by Dynkin diagrams. Auslander–Reiten theory then studies the relations among indecomposable representations.

Root systems encode the reflection geometry underlying semisimple Lie theory. This development connects positive roots and simple reflections to Weyl groups, Coxeter systems, chambers and longest elements. Dynkin diagrams organize the Cartan–Killing classification, while integral root data retain the information needed for algebraic groups. Explicit numbering and worked families make the combinatorial classification usable in later representation-theoretic constructions.

Partitions and Young tableaux organize the representations of symmetric groups. This development constructs permutation modules, Young symmetrizers and Specht modules, then proves their classification, standard-basis and hook-length results. Character calculations lead through symmetric functions and the Frobenius characteristic to Schur–Weyl duality. Brauer algebras extend the relationship between tensor powers and group actions to orthogonal and symplectic groups.

Semisimple algebras are built from simple modules and matrix algebras over division rings. This development assembles the Artin–Wedderburn classification with uniqueness, isotypic decompositions and double-centralizer results. Central simple algebras, tensor products and Skolem–Noether then lead to splitting fields and the Brauer group. These structures provide a common algebraic foundation for character theory, classical representations and arithmetic invariants.

Spin representations reveal symmetries of orthogonal groups that cannot be obtained from tensor powers of the standard representation alone. This development builds Clifford algebras, Pin and Spin groups, and their double covers, then constructs spin and half-spin modules. Low-dimensional exceptional isomorphisms, real Clifford algebras and triality provide concrete structure. The resulting representations connect quadratic forms, Lie theory and geometry.
tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/UniversalCovers: A universal cover replaces a space by a simply connected covering space while retaining its fundamental-group symmetry. For path-connected, locally path-connected and semilocally simply connected spaces, this development constructs universal covers and deck transformations, then proves lifting criteria and the correspondence between connected covers and subgroups of the fundamental group. Higher homotopy comparisons and applications extend the picture. The theory provides a geometric bridge between local topology and global algebraic invariants.
